While deep learning has recently demonstrated exceptional performance in various medical imaging tasks, it typically relies on supervised learning, necessitating fully annotated datasets. Consequently, this paper introduces a novel framework for medical image segmentation that leverages weakly supervised learning. We propose a new approach to learn from partial annotations, termed "label-free weakly-supervised learning." This method utilizes weakly labeled data that includes only a few annotated regions of interest (ROIs) alongside a set of bounding boxes. This research broadens the scope of algebraic automata theory and the application of tree automata to logic. in physics, particularly in describing graphene and its derivatives. This work introduces a novel class of soliton solutions for the Dirac equation featuring a delta potential. These solutions are characterized by a non-zero spinor component at the origin, a feature that cannot be achieved with other soliton configurations. We demonstrate that solutions with opposite charges exhibit distinct behaviors at the origin, where either the electron or the soliton remains localized. underlying network topology. While the degree distribution is a standard topological feature, it fails to capture information regarding the distribution of higher-order moments. The entropic index serves as a normalized metric for these higher-order moments, and its corresponding entropy measure is known as the Tsallis entropy. This study investigates the application of Tsallis entropy to examine correlations within networks. We introduce the Tsallis entropy of a path, which quantifies the uncertainty in the next node's position along a trajectory. Using this metric, we analyze the uncertainty of node transitions in real-world networks. Our findings indicate that networks with higher Tsallis entropy exhibit greater uncertainty in their topological structure. Furthermore, we observe that the Tsallis entropy of a path can be estimated with high accuracy using only the first two nodes. This estimation accuracy is significantly greater than what is achievable using the degree distribution alone. Consequently, our results demonstrate that Tsallis entropy offers a distinct and valuable perspective on network structure. Finally, we illustrate how Tsallis entropy can be utilized to predict the next node in a path. To our knowledge, this work represents the first instance of using Tsallis entropy for next-step prediction. Our approach achieves accuracy comparable to methods based on degree distributions and outperforms other techniques relying on higher-order moments. This suggests that Tsallis entropy is a promising tool for analyzing and predicting network properties. We anticipate that this work will inspire further research into Tsallis entropy applications in network science. To facilitate this, we have released our code and data at https://github.com/abhishekprakash1994/Next-step-prediction. We present a novel family of supersymmetric black holes characterized by a single complex scalar field, the dynamics of which are governed by a hypermultiplet potential. This proposed phase transition is characterized by a shift in the black hole entropy, and we provide a detailed discussion of this phenomenon. Additionally, we examine the supersymmetric phase diagram of the black holes, which is governed by the black hole potential and the R-symmetry subgroup parameters. We observe that the phase diagram exhibits a rich structure, displaying a complex interplay between the various parameters. This work establishes a foundation for future investigations into supersymmetric black holes in four-dimensional gauged supergravity. In conclusion, we anticipate that our results will advance our comprehension of supersymmetric black holes and their holographic duals in four-dimensional gauged supergravity. This view is bolstered by the observation that the only experimentally confirmed lepton flavor symmetry is the baryon minus lepton number ($B-L$), which is also the accidentally conserved global symmetry at the renormalizable level in the Standard Model. This text examines the most straightforward extension of the Standard Model that incorporates quantum gravity, known as the Minimal Standard Model (MSM). In the MSM, all global symmetries except $B-L$ are violated, leading to the generation of baryon and lepton number violating operators at the Planck scale. These operators are capable of producing stable, weakly interacting massive particles (WIMPs), specifically "cosmons," which serve as viable dark matter candidates. Furthermore, the study explores the phenomenological implications of these operators, including their effects on the early universe and current cosmological observations. Finally, the work investigates the potential for detecting these operators through neutrino experiments. The analysis concludes that the MSM offers a compelling framework for understanding the origins of neutrino masses and the nature of dark matter. Consequently, it is recommended that both neutrino and dark matter experiments expand their search capabilities to include these cosmons. This recommendation is supported by a novel method for searching for cosmons using existing data from the NOvA experiment. Additionally, the paper provides a comprehensive review of the current status of the MSM, covering the latest constraints on cosmons and the prospects for their future detection. The findings suggest that the MSM is a promising candidate for explaining the origins of neutrino masses and dark matter, and that the search for cosmons is a viable avenue for both neutrino and dark matter research. We introduce the concept of quantum causal nonlocality, defined as the minimum distance between a quantum causal model and a nonlocal quantum correlation. Our analysis reveals that quantum causal nonlocality aligns perfectly with quantum causality: any nonlocal correlation can be approximated by a quantum causal model to any desired degree of precision. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this approximation can be achieved using a single-qubit quantum causal model. These findings suggest that quantum causal nonlocality and quantum causal models are intrinsically linked, indicating that quantum causality arises from the nonlocality of quantum correlations. Consequently, we conclude that quantum causal nonlocality offers a more appropriate characterization of quantum causality than quantum locality. Finally, we explore the implications of these results for the Bell-Kochen-Specker theorem. We show that the Bell-Kochen-Specker theorem can be reformulated as a quantum causal nonlocality theorem, thereby establishing a significant connection between the Bell-Bohm-Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen theorem and the Bell-Kochen-Specker theorem. Additionally, we provide a quantum causal model-based explanation for the Greenberger-Van-der-Merch-Ghose-Spekkens theorem. Our work confirms that quantum causality is a fundamental and universal aspect of quantum mechanics. By unifying the Bell-Bohm-Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen and Bell-Kochen-Specker theorems, our results offer a new perspective on the foundations of quantum mechanics. Ultimately, we believe that quantum causal nonlocality will prove to be a powerful new tool for advancing quantum theory. In this setting, a decision-maker (DM) must decide whether to gather information before making a choice, balancing the costs and benefits of such decisions. The DM faces an adversarial environment where the adversary observes the information acquisition policy and adjusts its own strategy to minimize the DM's utility. We demonstrate that information acquisition policies in this adversarial context can be characterized as a zero-sum game, allowing for the identification of optimal policies through a saddle point. Furthermore, we introduce a model-free, model-based, and model-based algorithm for learning these optimal policies. Our approach utilizes a value function to evaluate the long-term value of acquiring information and a utility function to assess the value of the decision itself. We prove that the parameter values converging during the learning process of these dual functions correspond to a saddle point, thereby yielding optimal policies for both the decision-maker and the adversary. Finally, we validate the effectiveness of our proposed dual-critic RL method through simulations involving a DM and an adversary operating within a social network. The results indicate that our approach successfully learns the optimal information acquisition policy for the DM. Additionally, we demonstrate that our dual-critic RL method outperforms existing state-of-the-art RL techniques in this adversarial environment. To our knowledge, this work represents the first application of dual-critic RL to learn optimal information acquisition policies under adversarial conditions. Using high-resolution near-infrared spectroscopy from the Keck Observatory, we measured the radial velocities of WASP 12, achieving a precision of 100 m/s. Power line communication (PLC) offers a promising solution by utilizing existing high-voltage infrastructure without the need for new cabling. Furthermore, the research assesses the impact of PSPAM on PLC spectral compliance and the resulting power loss. The findings indicate that PSPAM is a viable solution for PLC applications, offering higher data rates with only a minor increase in power loss. Finally, the paper outlines the implementation of PSPAM using a straightforward and efficient digital signal processing technique. Ultimately, PSPAM presents a promising alternative for PLC applications, particularly in scenarios where maximizing data transmission rate is critical. from a deeper principle: the Standard Model's (SM) Higgs potential is the most natural choice for a scalar field because its parameters are protected by symmetry. This protection allows the potential to be flat at the origin, enabling the vacuum expectation value (VEV) to emerge dynamically. Consequently, the Higgs VEV is not an independent parameter but is instead linked to the value of the Higgs field at its minimum. In this framework, the Higgs acts as a pseudo-Nambu-Goldstone boson (pNGB) resulting from the spontaneous breaking of an approximate global symmetry. This perspective offers a natural explanation for the hierarchy between the Higgs VEV and the Planck scale, as well as for the smallness of the top quark mass. We examine the implications of this view for the SM's Yukawa sector, proposing that the Yukawa coupling matrix also stems from a symmetry argument. This approach predicts a novel family of fermions, the "Yukawaons," which interact with SM quarks and leptons. We analyze the phenomenological consequences of these new fermions and their potential role in explaining neutrino masses. Furthermore, we outline a UV completion for this scenario, demonstrating that the SM Higgs can be identified as a pNGB within a spontaneously broken, extended gauge symmetry. This model features a new $SU(2)$ gauge group with two new gauge bosons and a new vector-like fermion doublet, the latter of which is essential for generating the Higgs pNGB. We find that the mass of this new vector-like fermion is tightly constrained by the requirement that the Higgs mass remains at 125 GeV. Finally, we discuss the phenomenological implications of these new particles and their possible connection to dark matter. This proposal represents a significant departure from conventional wisdom, suggesting that the SM Higgs VEV is not a free parameter but is instead fixed by a symmetry argument. This insight could pave the way for a more profound understanding of the origins of particle masses and the structure of the SM. We contend that this work establishes a new paradigm for addressing the gauge hierarchy problem. We name this approach the "Higgs Naturalness Principle." We introduce a novel method for calculating these decomposed isogenies, which is both rapid and suitable for key recovery in the supersingular key encapsulation mechanism (SS-KEM). This approach is particularly effective for determining endomorphisms within the 2-Sylow subgroup, an operation essential for the Bost-Chabauty algorithm that enables efficient and complete recovery of isogeny paths. Additionally, we outline a strategy for integrating this method into a generalized isogeny-based key encapsulation mechanism (GKEM). Experimental results demonstrate that the Bost-Chabautu algorithm combined with our new technique achieves performance that is significantly faster than existing solutions. Specifically, in the SS-KEM context, the isogeny path computation is accelerated by a factor of $10^4$ to $10^6$, while the isogeny evaluation is improved by a factor of $10^2$ to $10^4$. Furthermore, our analysis of the GKEM shows that the method is feasible for parameters up to 256 bits. Finally, we examine the security of this new method, proving that it is secure under the assumption that the endomorphism ring isomorphism problem is hard. This scenario corresponds to a rank-constrained projection onto the cone of positive semi-definite matrices. This study investigates the statistical likelihood of such a model by examining the distribution of the amplitude parameter $A_s$ and the power spectrum index $n_s$. Our findings indicate that the non-Gaussian model remains statistically probable within the $1\sigma$ confidence interval, contingent upon the specific cosmological model employed. Consequently, we recommend that the non-Gaussian model be treated as an alternative to $\Lambda$CDM, with parameters calibrated to match the $\Lambda$CDM predictions. Drawing on a design ethnography of TikTok, we investigate how this mechanism influences user behavior. Our analysis reveals that the play button serves as a navigational aid, enabling users to quickly skip unwanted content and return to their previous position. This design choice conserves users' cognitive and emotional resources, allowing them to maintain their flow state and sustain long-term engagement. Consequently, we propose the concept of "in-between navigation" to describe this behavior. Our findings offer insights into the design of media consumption applications and highlight the ethical implications of these attention-driven design patterns. Ultimately, we argue that designers must be more transparent about the specific design decisions that shape user behavior. We hope this research encourages the development of more ethical design practices and prompts a critical examination of the underlying motivations behind such choices. This study examines the magnetic properties of the material across various Ni-site vacancies ($\delta$) using neutron diffraction and muon spin rotation/relaxation ($\mu$SR) techniques. At a Ni vacancy concentration of $\delta$ = 0.25, the system exhibits a two-dimensional (2D) spin liquid state below 10 K, characterized by a non-uniformly distributed vacancy pattern. In contrast, for $\delta$ = 0.5, where vacancies are uniformly distributed, the material undergoes a 2D antiferromagnetic (AF) transition at approximately 1.5 K. Notably, the magnetic susceptibility ($\chi$) displays a Curie-Weiss-like temperature dependence with a positive Weiss constant ($\theta$) of roughly 10 K, indicating significant magnetic frustration. Furthermore, the temperature dependence of $\chi$ aligns with the theoretical predictions for the 2D triangular-lattice Ising model. These findings underscore the critical role of the spatial distribution of Ni$^{2+}$ vacancies in governing the magnetic behavior of Ni$_{3-\delta}$NiTeO$_{6}$. Additionally, the observed 2D AFM transition at $\delta$ = 0.5 is consistent with the 2D Ising model, suggesting that the Ising model is applicable to this triangular-lattice system. Consequently, the interplay between magnetic frustration and the Ising model in Na$_{4-\delta}$NiTeO$_{6}$ offers a compelling explanation for its unique magnetic phase transitions. Finally, the material's potential for magnetic refrigeration is also discussed. These results establish Na$_{4-\delta}$NiTeO$_{6}$ as a promising candidate for investigating magnetic frustration and the interplay between the Ising model and frustration within triangular-lattice structures. This paper introduces a new approach to address the time-dependent wave equation by employing a discontinuous Galerkin (dG) method in time, utilizing the semi-discrete formulation of the problem. This strategy eliminates the necessity to solve large, dense mass matrices. We demonstrate that this method is equivalent to applying the Crank-Nicolson scheme to the second-order form of the wave equation using the finite element method (FEM) with linear basis functions in time. Furthermore, we establish second-order accuracy in time for the semi-discrete dG solution and present numerical results comparing it with the standard Crank-Nicolson scheme. Additionally, we extend the dG method to the full discretization using any consistent discretization for the spatial problem, with a particular focus on the finite difference method. Numerical experiments validate the theoretical findings, showing that the proposed dG scheme achieves second-order accuracy in time and can be efficiently implemented using the fast Fourier transform. Finally, we apply this time-only dG scheme to the finite difference wave equation to solve the initial value problem for the three-dimensional wave equation on a Cartesian grid. The results confirm that the dG scheme yields second-order accuracy in time and can be computed efficiently using the fast Fourier transform. The corresponding code is available on GitHub. The proposed dG scheme offers a viable alternative to the Crank-Nicolson scheme, as it avoids solving large linear systems and instead relies on a simple explicit update formula. Consequently, this approach is well-suited for applications requiring the solution of the wave equation in three dimensions. The paper concludes with a discussion of the method's potential applications. the proliferation of connected devices has created significant challenges regarding data security and privacy. The Internet of Body Areas (IoB) represents a specialized domain within IoT, where vast quantities of personal information are gathered from wearable devices and other smart health systems. This data often contains sensitive details, such as medical histories, that require robust protection. However, current research on securing IoB data remains limited. This paper introduces a novel framework designed to safeguard data within the IoB environment. The proposed solution leverages blockchain technology to ensure data integrity and privacy. Specifically, we present a blockchain-based architecture that enables the secure storage of health records, allowing for selective access by authorized users. Furthermore, we provide a detailed analysis of the framework's security properties and evaluate its performance. Finally, we discuss the framework's applicability to the IoB context. Our findings demonstrate that blockchain offers a viable and effective mechanism for protecting data in the IoB. Additionally, we contend that this research holds substantial value for the broader scientific community. The framework is implemented using Hyperledger Fabric, a prominent blockchain platform. We have deployed this solution on a testbed comprising Raspberry Pi devices and smartphones to validate its functionality. The results confirm that the proposed framework successfully addresses the security and privacy challenges inherent to IoB data. Consequently, we conclude that integrating blockchain technology is essential for securing data in the IoB. This research paves the way for future advancements in blockchain applications within the IoB. The source code for the Hyperledger Fabric implementation is publicly accessible at: https://github.com/ahmedmohamed1994/Blockchain-IoB. This work was presented at the 2021 IEEE International Conference on Blockchain & Blockchain in Cloud Systems (BCS). This paper examines the factors influencing the timing of electricity transmission investments within a European framework. It analyzes the impact of these factors on investment decisions using a stylized model of electricity market competition, where grid owners act as public monopolists. The study further explores how these elements evolve as the degree of renewable penetration increases. The findings indicate that both renewable penetration and the cost of new lines influence the timing of expansion; however, while line cost reductions can delay investments, rising renewable penetration accelerates them. Consequently, policy interventions aimed at lowering the costs of electricity transmission investments could be highly effective in facilitating grid expansion. Additionally, the analysis reveals that transmission expansion is more likely to be delayed when line costs are high and renewable penetration is low. This scenario typically occurs in regions with limited renewable potential, such as Northern Europe. Therefore, it is crucial to prioritize transmission expansion in these areas to support the broader integration of renewables across the continent. Finally, the study suggests that transmission pricing mechanisms that internalize the costs of generation expansion could help prevent investment delays. This approach would benefit both the market and society by reducing the need for new generation capacity and the associated costs. However, implementing this pricing mechanism may require substantial adjustments to the current EU framework. To address this, the paper proposes a new pricing mechanism that accounts for generation expansion costs while remaining compatible with the existing EU regulatory structure. This proposed mechanism is expected to accelerate transmission expansion, thereby facilitating the integration of renewable energy. The analysis demonstrates that this new pricing structure is feasible and can be implemented under current EU rules. Ultimately, the study concludes that while the new pricing mechanism is essential for achieving the EU's climate goals, it must be complemented by policies that reduce the costs of electricity generation and transmission investments. This combination will help ensure that expansion decisions are made promptly, enabling the full integration of renewable energy across the European Union. Physics (HEP) has become increasingly competitive, with only a small fraction of PhD graduates securing positions. This paper examines the current landscape of HEP job advertisements and offers insights into prevailing hiring trends. The findings are particularly relevant to the U.S. Department of Energy's Office of Science, which oversees the majority of American HEP institutions and holds responsibility for their personnel. Additionally, the study discusses the implications of these trends for HEP institutions, the workforce, and the next generation of physicists. The analysis draws upon a survey of HEP career resources, existing literature on the field, and the author's personal experience. The paper is structured into three main sections: first, an overview of the existing career system; second, an analysis of job postings from 2010 to 2021; and finally, a discussion of the implications for the future. The conclusion suggests that the current career system may be failing to meet the needs of both institutions and employees, necessitating a reevaluation of the roles and responsibilities of HEP institutions and their staff. Furthermore, the paper calls for further research into the career trajectories of HEP PhD graduates and the broader workforce. Ultimately, the goal is to provide a resource that aids HEP institutions and their leadership in making informed decisions regarding their workforce. The core challenge lies in balancing exploration and exploitation: the agent must gather sufficient data to locate the optimal action while minimizing the regret incurred during the decision-making process. We analyze the regret bounds for two distinct scenarios: (i) when the expected reward function is convex, and (ii) when the reward function is merely smooth. Our findings indicate that in the convex case, regret can be bounded by a constant, whereas in the general smooth case, regret is bounded by the logarithm of the horizon length. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our algorithms are optimal by proving a lower bound that matches our regret upper bound up to a constant factor. Finally, we validate the effectiveness of our proposed algorithms through numerical experiments using both synthetic and real-world datasets. The source code for our algorithms is accessible at https://github.com/AnirbanMukherjee1998/ActivePureExploration. This work is a condensed version of the full paper: "Active Pure Exploration in Contextual Bandits: A Generalized Zero-Regret Solution," which can be found at https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.00999.
Keywords: Active Pure Exploration, Contextual Bandits, Smooth Convex Functions, Regret Analysis, Lower Bound, Synthetic and Real-world Data.

This study introduces a scheme utilizing a laser plasma interaction within a plasma channel to generate a high-energy electron beam. The process begins with a high-intensity, short-pulse laser creating a plasma channel characterized by a specific electron density profile. Subsequently, a low-density, high-intensity laser is focused into this channel to produce a wakefield. The resulting plasma wave accelerates electrons to a final energy of 1.5 GeV over a distance of 10 cm. X-ray surveys have identified numerous X-ray-selected galaxy clusters with redshifts ranging from $z=0.5$ to $z=1.5$. This study utilizes the publicly available XMM-Newton data from the W-CDF-S survey to investigate the X-ray surface brightness profiles of these clusters. We employ a new method to determine the core radius ($r_c$) and total integrated flux ($S_{\rm tot}$) for each cluster, subsequently comparing these values against those derived from standard fitting techniques. Our analysis reveals that the X-ray surface brightness profiles of W-CDF-S clusters are generally well-described by a $\beta$ model, with $r_c$ values typically falling between 100 and 200 kpc. Furthermore, we examine the relationship between $r_c$ and $S_{\rm tot}$, finding that the correlation between these two parameters is stronger when $r_c$ is derived using the proposed method rather than the conventional approach. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for the scaling relations of X-ray selected clusters. These results offer valuable insights into the characteristics of X-ray selected clusters and the potential of the presented method for estimating $r_c$ and $S_{\rm tot}$. Additionally, the methodology is applicable to other X-ray selected clusters, including those from the ROSAT, XMM-Newton, and Chandra surveys. The associated Python code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi1995/Estimating_core_radius_and_total_flux. The analysis examines how the interplay among the eigenvalues of the diffusion matrix, the linear reaction matrix, and the nonlinearity's Jacobian drives pattern formation. Specifically, nonlinearities that are monotone decreasing in each variable can induce Turing patterns even without satisfying the standard conditions typically required for scalar systems with diagonal diffusion. The study employed a $3 \times 3 \times 1$ supercell containing 48 atoms, with the topmost Fe layer (Fe$_1$) removed to simulate surface conditions. Safety Networks (PSN) are anticipated to leverage the integration of Terahertz (THz) and Reconfigurable Intelligent Surfaces (RIS) to deliver high-capacity, low-latency, and ultra-reliable communications. This study investigates the performance of RIS-assisted THz PSN by accounting for atmospheric absorption, beam squint, and diffraction. We introduce a novel algorithm that jointly optimizes RIS phase shifts and transmitter (Tx) beamforming to maximize the achievable rate. The proposed approach utilizes a multi-stage optimization strategy: first, it determines Tx beamforming weights to maximize the rate of a single-user link, followed by an algorithm to calculate the necessary phase shifts for the RIS. Simulation results demonstrate that this method achieves significant performance gains compared to baseline schemes. Furthermore, the study analyzes the impact of RIS element count and THz beamforming techniques on achievable rates, revealing that the proposed algorithm exhibits superior performance relative to existing works. Finally, we examine the effects of atmospheric absorption and beam squint on the achievable rate. Our findings indicate that while beam squint negatively affects performance, the proposed algorithm maintains robust rate capabilities even under severe atmospheric absorption conditions. These results suggest that the proposed algorithm is well-suited for future PSN applications operating in the THz band. Additionally, the research offers valuable insights for designing RIS-assisted THz PSN systems. The source code for this work is available at: https://github.com/ChenYuan1999/THz-RIS-PSN. a pervasive phenomenon in daily life, yet its mechanisms remain poorly understood. This study investigates the POTP experienced during the waiting period for a train. We hypothesize that POTP arises from the brain's predictive coding system, where the mind anticipates future events. Consequently, we propose that the degree of time passage is inversely related to the accuracy of this prediction. To test this, we conducted a survey involving 100 participants, asking them to estimate the elapsed time of their actual waiting experiences. Our results indicate that the perceived time is significantly shorter than the actual elapsed time, and that perceived time is approximately 85% of the actual duration. Furthermore, we found that the perceived time is not merely a function of the actual time but also depends on the margin of error between perceived and actual durations. These findings support our hypothesis that reduced prediction error leads to less perceived time passage. Additionally, we observed that the perceived time for the first waiting segment is longer than for subsequent segments of equal actual duration, suggesting a learning effect. This effect is attributed to the brain refining its predictive models with each experience, thereby increasing prediction accuracy and reducing the sense of time passing. Our results offer insights into POTP within real-world contexts and have practical applications, such as in the design of user interfaces. For instance, UIs could incorporate features to minimize perceived time, such as displaying progress bars or sending periodic updates, which could enhance user experience. This work is part of a broader effort to understand POTP in various scenarios, including driving, gaming, and social interactions. The dataset and code are accessible at https://github.com/abhishekjain10/Perception-of-Time-Passage.

By analyzing the absorption features of the Lyman-alpha (Ly$\alpha$) forest, we can investigate the spatial arrangement of this gas around galaxies at redshifts $z\sim2-3$. This study utilizes a sample of 11 galaxies from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) at $z\sim2.3$, selected for their proximity to the Lyman limit (LL) of their host galaxies. We calculated the Ly$\alpha$ forest transmission function, $T_{Ly\alpha}$, for each galaxy, defining the LL region as the wavelength range from LL-100 to LL+100 Å. Our analysis reveals that $T_{Ly\alpha}$ is significantly lower for galaxies with higher stellar masses, indicating that the CGM is more compact around massive systems. Additionally, the transmission function exhibits a strong dependence on the redshift of the absorber. We propose that the observed variation in $T_{Ly\alpha}$ stems from the proximity of the host galaxy to the absorber. Using a semi-analytic model, we estimated the distance between the absorber and the host galaxy, finding that the CGM is located at approximately 100 kpc from the host. This distance aligns with the scale of the CGM, suggesting that the absorber resides within the CGM. Consequently, our findings demonstrate that the CGM is more compact around massive galaxies and is situated at a distance comparable to its own scale. Furthermore, we confirmed that the CGM is more prevalent around galaxies with higher stellar masses. This study demonstrates that applying a perpendicular magnetic field to a 2D ferromagnet induces a significant change in its magnetic order, specifically within the 2D ferromagnetic semiconductor MnBi$_2$Te$_4$. By integrating transport measurements with first-principles calculations, we identify a magnetic phase transition from a ferromagnetic state to a canted antiferromagnetic state under an applied field of approximately 10 T. The emergence of this new magnetic phase results in the suppression of long-range ferromagnetic order, causing the magnetic moment to tilt away from the c-axis. Furthermore, we observe that the magnetoresistance exhibits a sign reversal at around 10 T, a phenomenon explained by the modified magnetic structure. These findings establish a foundation for investigating magnetic phase transitions in 2D ferromagnets using a magnetic field. Additionally, the tunability of the 2D magnetic state offers promising prospects for developing novel spintronic devices. This topological phase can be further modulated by varying the MnBi$_2$Te$_4$ thickness. Consequently, our findings provide a pathway to achieve a tunable topological Weyl semimetal phase in 2D ferromagnets. This work also extends the understanding of magnetic phase transitions in 2D ferromagnets, which are crucial for the development of next-generation spintronic devices. Ultimately, this research paves the way for exploring novel topological phases in 2D ferromagnets. The primary findings demonstrate that a point is regular if and only if it is feasible, lies within the interior of the domain, and satisfies a generalized form of the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker conditions. This paper introduces a new framework for analyzing quantum coherence based on an operational principle: the maximum amount of coherence that can be extracted from a single state into multiple states through incoherent operations. We propose a family of coherence measures satisfying this criterion and demonstrate that these measures are mathematically equivalent to the Rains relative entropy of asymmetry when applied to pure states. Furthermore, we establish an upper limit for single-shot coherence distillation and confirm that our measures achieve this bound. For mixed states, we derive analytic lower bounds on coherence distillation using semidefinite programming. Additionally, we examine the relationship between coherence distillation and distillation in the broader context of state conversion via incoherent operations, proving that any mixed-state transformation achievable in the latter can also be realized by first distilling the state and subsequently transforming the resulting ensemble. Finally, we analyze the monotonicity of our measures under incoherent operations and investigate the concept of incoherent distinguishability. These findings offer a novel perspective on quantifying and understanding quantum coherence. Moreover, the measures presented here may find applications in other quantum information processing tasks, such as distinguishing between incoherent states. The proposed framework is versatile and can be extended to other resource theories utilizing similar resource conversion rules. Consequently, this work may inspire the development of new resource theories and enhance our understanding of quantum correlations. The proofs for all results are provided in the supplementary material. We anticipate that these results will advance the field of quantum information processing. aryonic matter in the Universe is thought to reside in the form of hot gas within galaxy clusters. However, the origin of this gas remains unclear, with the most plausible theory suggesting it was accreted from the intergalactic medium (IGM). **Aims.** This study investigates the IGM's contribution to the intracluster medium (ICM) by analyzing the IGM's characteristics and the mechanisms driving gas accretion. **Methods.** We examine the IGM's properties using the latest observational data and compare them with predictions from the standard $\Lambda$CDM model. Furthermore, we employ a semi-analytical model to determine the IGM mass captured by galaxy clusters and the specific fraction of this mass that is accreted. **Results.** Our findings indicate that the IGM is predominantly composed of baryons, with a mass fraction of approximately 15% residing in the warm-hot intergalactic medium (WHIM). We observe that the IGM is primarily distributed in the warm phase, with a mean temperature of roughly $10^5$ K. Additionally, the IGM is mainly found in the intergalactic medium (IM), accounting for about 80% of its mass. The accretion process is primarily driven by the gravitational potential of galaxy clusters, which is responsible for approximately 70% of the accretion. **Conclusions.** We conclude that the IGM plays a significant role in the formation of the ICM. Furthermore, the gravitational potential of galaxy clusters is the primary driver of IGM accretion. These results support the hypothesis that IGM accretion is a crucial mechanism for the formation of the ICM. **Keywords:** galaxies: clusters: intracluster medium, galaxies: clusters: general properties, galaxies: intracluster medium, intergalactic medium, intergalactic medium: WHIM, intergalactic medium: IM, intergalactic medium: CGM, intergalactic medium: WHIM, intergalactic medium: IM, intergalactic medium: CGM.

Finally, the results are presented as lower limits on the decay lengths for both $B^0_s\to \mu^+ \mu^-$ and $B_s^\pm\to \mu^\pm \mu^-$, utilizing the measured decay widths and masses. These systems are thought to be the remnants of planetary systems that were disrupted and accreted onto the WDs during their post-main sequence evolution. However, the specific mechanisms driving this disruption and the timescales involved remain uncertain. This study investigates the orbital evolution of a planetesimal within a binary system, where the WD is the primary star and a compact companion (such as a white dwarf, neutron star, or black hole) acts as the perturber. We examine how the companion influences the precession of a planetesimal's orbit, potentially causing it to cross the Roche limit and be subsequently destroyed. Our analysis covers various orbital configurations, including coplanar, eccentric, and retrograde scenarios. Our findings indicate that the companion can induce the planetesimal to oscillate between prograde and retrograde orbits, potentially leading to Roche limit crossing. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the companion can cause a planetesimal to transition between prograde and retrograde states even without crossing the Roche limit. These transitions can occur on timescales of a few million years, which is comparable to the typical age of WD systems. Consequently, our results suggest that the companion star plays a crucial role in the pollution of white dwarfs. Additionally, we show that a planetesimal can be ejected from the system due to companion-induced perturbations. Finally, we discuss the implications of these results for WD pollution and ejection events. This study is the first to explore the orbital evolution of a planetesimal in a WD system featuring a compact companion. We hope that our findings will aid in understanding the origins of WD pollution and the ejection mechanisms of planets from such systems. Our analysis reveals that the number of iterations depends on the restricted isometry constant (RIC) of $\mathbf{A}$, the sparsity level $k$, and the $\ell_2$-norm of $\mathbf{x}$. Specifically, we prove that the number of iterations is upper-bounded by $O\left(\frac{1}{1-\delta_{k}}\log\frac{\|\mathbf{x}\|_2}{\epsilon}\right)$, where $\epsilon$ denotes the desired accuracy. This result is consistent with prior findings in the literature. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 presents the ISTA algorithm for sparse recovery; Section 3 analyzes its convergence; Section 4 compares its performance with other algorithms; and Section 5 provides numerical simulations. The paper concludes with a discussion of our findings. The source code is available at https://github.com/ahmedmohamed1/ISTA.

a frequency shift for a particle oscillating around an equilibrium point, dependent on its total energy. This frequency varies with energy, meaning it is not constant but rather depends on the oscillation's amplitude. In this work, we examine a similar phenomenon within quantum mechanics. We demonstrate that the frequency of a quantum particle in an anharmonic potential also shifts due to its energy (or equivalently, its quantum number), differing from the frequency of the corresponding classical oscillation with the same energy. Furthermore, we show that this quantum frequency is amplitude-dependent, thereby confirming the validity of the frequency shift. Additionally, we discuss the implications of this result for the equivalence between classical and quantum descriptions. Finally, we illustrate the observed frequency shift using the inverted harmonic oscillator as a specific example. This model is particularly significant because it represents a classical particle that can escape to infinity, yet the quantum counterpart is trapped in a discrete set of energy levels. This provides a compelling demonstration of the shift between classical and quantum frequencies. Moreover, this shift is relevant to the quantum treatment of the hydrogen atom, where the electron's energy levels are quantized despite the proton's classical instability. Our analysis confirms that the frequency of a quantum electron bound to a proton is well-defined and discrete, differing from the classical frequency of an electron orbiting a proton at the same energy level. This finding has important implications for the stability of atoms and the quantum nature of matter. Ultimately, our results highlight the fundamental differences between classical and quantum mechanics and the unique properties of quantum systems. Planet Imager (GPI) and the Extremely Large Telescope (ELT), are poised to deliver high-contrast images of exoplanets. However, the Earth's turbulent atmosphere severely restricts the performance of these ground-based systems. To address this, adaptive optics (AO) is employed to correct wavefront distortions, enabling the creation of diffraction-limited images. This study details the development of a novel AO system designed for a 20-meter telescope. The system utilizes a 1-meter diameter deformable mirror (DM) featuring 1,536 actuators and a 1.5-degree field of view (FOV) Shack-Hartmann wavefront sensor (WFS) equipped with 1,024 sub-apertures. The control loop operates at 1,000 Hz, with a latency of 100 microseconds. The control architecture comprises a linear closed-loop controller, a nonlinear closed-loop controller, and a Kalman filter. The nonlinear controller incorporates a 100th-order polynomial function, while the Kalman filter is implemented as a state-space Kalman filter. The system's performance is evaluated using the Strehl ratio, contrast, and the full width at half maximum (FWHM) of the point spread function (PSF). While this phenomenon is typically modeled using the master equation, which describes the time evolution of the system's density matrix, we propose an alternative framework based on the Wigner function. This approach enables the visualization of decoherence dynamics and the transition from quantum to classical behavior. We demonstrate that the Wigner function offers insights into decoherence that are not immediately apparent from the density matrix alone. Specifically, we show that the density matrix's off-diagonal elements correspond to the Wigner function along a specific line, while the diagonal elements of the density matrix are recovered by integrating the positive regions of the Wigner function. Furthermore, we illustrate how the dynamics of the Wigner function reveal decoherence mechanisms, such as the diffusion of positive values into negative ones. Finally, we provide a physical interpretation of the master equation derived from the Wigner function formulation. This perspective highlights the Wigner function as a valuable tool for analyzing decoherence, particularly in scenarios where the master equation is difficult to derive or solve. Additionally, the Wigner function facilitates the investigation of decoherence in non-Markovian contexts. Consequently, this work aims to establish the Wigner function as an essential component of the standard toolkit for studying decoherence. Additionally, we present a straightforward method for simulating the Wigner function of a quantum system interacting with a bosonic bath, applicable to both Markovian and non-Markovian conditions. This method relies on the observation that the Wigner function of a system coupled to a bosonic bath can be expressed as a mixture of Wigner functions associated with the bath's Fock states. Moreover, the Wigner function can be reconstructed from the master equation's solutions for each Fock state, which can be computed using established methods. This approach is particularly advantageous for simulating decoherence in non-Markovian settings, where the Wigner function is otherwise challenging to calculate. We validate the accuracy of this method by comparing its results with exact numerical simulations. Additionally, we show that the method can be extended to incorporate system nonlinearity. Finally, we discuss the potential of this method for simulating decoherence in various systems, including those involving fermionic baths. This work was published in Phys. Rev. **1. Introduction**
Summarizing dialogue is a complex task due to the unordered nature of conversations. While prior research has primarily focused on generating summaries from dialogue data, this work proposes simple methods to improve summary ordering by integrating ordering information into neural summarization models. Specifically, we introduce two straightforward strategies: (i) adding a BERT module to predict sentence permutations and (R)Eplacing RNNs with Attention mechanisms. We assess the effectiveness of these approaches on the DialogueSum dataset. The proposed methods yield superior results compared to strong baselines, as confirmed by both automatic metrics and human evaluation. Additionally, we provide an analysis of how sentence ordering influences summary quality. Finally, we release our code and dataset to support future research.

**2. Related Work**
Recent studies have explored summarizing dialogues using various neural architectures, including LSTM, Transformer, and BERT. However, most of these approaches rely on either a single model or an ensemble of multiple models. In contrast, our method leverages two simple strategies to enhance summary ordering, achieving state-of-the-art performance on the DialogueSum dataset. Our code and data can be accessed at: https://github.com/ymudigk/Ordering-Information-in-Neural-Summarization.

**3. Method**
We employ a standard encoder-decoder framework for dialogue summarization, utilizing a BERT-based encoder and a Transformer-based decoder. To improve performance, we introduce two simple strategies: (i) adding a BERT module to predict sentence permutations and (R)Eplacing RNNs with Attention mechanisms. We evaluate these approaches against other state-of-the-art models on the DialogueSum dataset. The code for our implementation is available at: https://github.com

the angle between the neutron's spin and its velocity vector is termed spin-dependent scattering. This effect is crucial for the operation of neutron choppers and monochromators, as well as for the spin polarization of neutrons. This paper presents a systematic investigation into the spin-dependent scattering of cold neutrons from various nuclei. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive analysis of the spin-dependent scattering cross-sections for all target nuclei, covering both the ground state and the first excited state. Our findings indicate that spin-dependent scattering is significant for several nuclei, including $^{10}$B, $^{14}$N, $^{16}$O, $^{18}$O, $^{19}$F, $^{23}$Na, $^{27}$Al, $^{31}$P, $^{35}$Cl, $^{39}$K, $^{40}$Ca, $^{42}$K, $^{43}$Ca, $^{45}$Sc, $^{47}$Ti, $^{49}$Ca, $^{51}$V, $^{59}$Co, and $^{63}$Cu. Furthermore, we demonstrate that spin-dependent scattering is negligible for most other nuclei. Finally, we examine the impact of spin-dependent scattering on the performance of a cold neutron chopper. Our results show that for certain nuclei, spin-dependent scattering can substantially influence the performance of neutron choppers and monochromators. Consequently, this effect must be considered when designing these devices. Our study is the first to systematically analyze and evaluate the influence of spin-dependent scattering on the performance of neutron choppers and monochromators. We anticipate that this work will be valuable for the design and performance analysis of neutron choppers and monochromators. Moreover, our study may aid in the search for new physics, such as electric dipole moments, in nuclei with a spin of 1/2. Finally, we believe that our study will be beneficial for the field of nuclear physics. The data presented in this work can be accessed at https://doi.org/10.17638/xraydata.3.1.

However, this paper demonstrates that for a specific category of models, termed "one-shot" models, maximizing training accuracy can actually be detrimental. We introduce the concept of one-shot models, which are defined by the property that their training accuracy converges to 1 as the sample size increases. We examine two straightforward examples: the one-shot perceptron and the one-shot kernel classifier. In both scenarios, we demonstrate that the generalization error behaves similarly to the error of a random classifier, even when the model is fully trained. This finding is established through an asymptotic analysis of the non-asymptotic error bounds for these one-shot classifiers. Furthermore, we show that the asymptotic behavior of the generalization error for one-shot classifiers differs from that of standard classifiers, such as the standard perceptron. Finally, we discuss the broader implications of these findings for both theoretical research and practical applications. Specifically, we highlight that the generalization error of one-shot models can be significantly reduced by employing a learning strategy that involves training the model on a subset of the available samples. This approach is particularly effective when the dataset is large, and we also provide a practical method for selecting the optimal subset size. The contributions of this work include: (i) the definition and identification of a new class of models known as one-shot classifiers, and (ii) the derivation of a novel generalization error bound for these models, which reveals that their generalization error is comparable to that of a random classifier. This insight is crucial for both theoretical understanding and practical application. To address this, we introduce a novel dimensionality reduction method called the dimensionality reduction algorithm based on the mean of the minimum distance (DRAM). DRAM utilizes the concept of the minimum distance from a data point to a cluster center, which is estimated using the mean absolute deviation (MAD) of distances from neighboring points. Introduction The task of obtaining hydrodynamic equations from the Boltzmann equation remains a central issue in kinetic theory. Typically, this involves expanding the solution in powers of the small parameter $\epsilon$, where $\epsilon \sim 1/\mathrm{Kn}$ and Kn is the Knudsen number. The resulting equations for the zeroth-order term are the standard Navier-Stokes equations. However, this standard procedure is not entirely straightforward. For instance, in the case of a single-component gas, the standard expansion yields the Navier-Stokes equations, but the equations for the first-order term are not hydrodynamic. In this paper, we demonstrate that an alternative approach to the standard expansion can produce hydrodynamic equations for both the zeroth and first orders. Specifically, the Navier-Stokes equations emerge for the zeroth-order term, while the equations for the first-order term take the form of modified Navier-Stokes equations that incorporate an additional nonlinear term. The derivation of the equations for the first-order term is facilitated by the fact that the nonlinear term satisfies a specific integral equation. This procedure is applicable to any system where the collision integral can be expressed as a quadratic form. In this work, we focus on a single-component gas, though the methodology is also applicable to polyatomic gases. designed to address the challenge of reconstructing a quantum state from incomplete data. The algorithm operates by classically optimizing the parameters of a parameterized quantum circuit, which in turn adjusts the quantum state. This process continues until the resulting state minimizes the distance between the reconstructed and the original target states. The approach is applicable to scenarios involving a limited number of measurement outcomes, known as weak data. We demonstrate that the hybrid nature of this algorithm enables it to achieve a reconstruction error scaling of $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{M})$, where $M$ represents the count of available data points. This scaling is optimal, matching the performance of the maximum likelihood estimator. Furthermore, we show that the algorithm's error scaling with respect to data points is independent of the Hilbert space dimension, and its error scaling regarding the number of circuit parameters is also optimal. Finally, we validate the algorithm's efficacy through numerical simulations on quantum state tomography tasks involving both pure and mixed states. These simulations confirm that the proposed algorithm outperforms the maximum likelihood estimator, particularly when dealing with weak data. Additionally, we illustrate that the algorithm can be implemented on near-term quantum hardware, such as those available on IBM's cloud platform.

However, DNNs remain vulnerable to more subtle, transferable attacks that were not explicitly targeted during the training phase. This paper introduces a novel approach designed to improve the robustness of DNNs against these untargeted transferable attacks. This work introduces a novel approach to solving convex optimization problems by employing a nonconvex algorithm. We demonstrate that the local minimality of a nonconvex problem can be achieved through a global constraint set, allowing the solution to be derived by iteratively refining this constraint. This method is applicable to a wide range of convex optimization tasks, including lasso, nuclear norm minimization, and $\ell_1$-norm minimization. Furthermore, we establish that the nonconvex problem, which contains the global solution set defined by the global constraint, is convergent. This convergence property ensures that any limit point of the iterative algorithm yields a locally optimal solution for the original convex problem. Finally, numerical experiments confirm the effectiveness of our proposed algorithm. In summary, this paper presents a new algorithm for convex optimization that leverages nonconvex techniques. The resulting method is nonconvex, enabling the utilization of existing nonconvex optimization tools. Additionally, the algorithm exhibits convergence, and its performance is validated through numerical testing. We anticipate that this work will inspire further research into the development of nonconvex algorithms for convex optimization. This paper introduces a novel framework designed to synthesize videos with coherent motion by explicitly modeling the correlation between adjacent frames. The core innovation lies in a new agent utility function that integrates both cooperative and competitive elements. The planning algorithm operates by iteratively maximizing each agent's utility through a series of linear quadratic programming problems, with the objective of approximating Nash equilibrium states. However, the sheer volume of data generated by these networks often exceeds the processing capabilities of conventional hardware. This paper presents a distributed approach for performing centrality analysis on large-scale social networks. The proposed system utilizes a peer-to-peer (P2P) architecture, where each node is assigned a specific subgraph. Furthermore, the system exhibits scalability, with a processing time that grows logarithmically as the network size increases. Finally, we compared our P2P solution against a centralized implementation, finding that the P2P approach outperforms the centralized one in terms of execution time. Our investigation reveals that NGC 2997 hosts a prominent, extended spiral arm structure, characterized by a distinct, elongated bar-like feature in the northern region. This feature exhibits a length-to-width ratio of approximately 2.5, a tilt angle of roughly 20 degrees relative to the major spiral arm, and a length scale of about 10 kpc. The bar-like structure displays a redshifted velocity profile, whereas the main spiral arm shows a blueshifted profile; this kinematic asymmetry suggests the presence of a large-scale warp in the gas disk. Additionally, we identified a significant chemical gradient across the galaxy, with a measured slope of -0.015 +/- 0.002 dex kpc^-1. This gradient is notably steeper than that observed in other nearby spiral galaxies, implying that NGC 2997 possesses a more extended disk compared to its peers. These findings indicate that NGC 2997 is a massive spiral galaxy featuring a large-scale disk warp and a prominent, elongated spiral arm structure. We propose that the bar-like feature in the northern region is a spiral arm perturbation resulting from a recent interaction with a smaller satellite galaxy. Such an interaction could account for the observed large-scale gas disk warp and the steeper-than-usual chemical gradient. Furthermore, the presence of this spiral perturbation may explain the unusually high number of star-forming regions in NGC 2997. Ultimately, our results suggest that spiral galaxies with large-scale disk warps and prominent spiral arm structures are more common than previously believed. Consequently, future studies of these galaxies are essential for understanding the role of disk warps in triggering star formation and the subsequent evolution of spiral galaxies. We introduce a novel approach that leverages the causal implications of a structural causal model (SCM) to estimate the effect of an intervention on a target variable, utilizing data from multiple observational studies where covariates may be missing in various ways. Our methodology employs a Bayesian framework to impute missing values, generating an ensemble of completed datasets. which a sender, possessing a prior distribution over a state of the world, selects a signaling scheme to maximize the receiver's expected payoff. In this framework, the sender can either reveal the state directly or disclose a signal correlated with the state, while a mechanism designer sets the rules for this communication. We demonstrate that the set of mechanisms achieving a specific payoff level forms a convex polytope, and any optimal mechanism can be expressed as a mixture of canonical forms. Specifically, we identify two such canonical mechanisms: a "pooling" mechanism where the state is hidden, and an "interim" mechanism where the mechanism designer reveals the state to agents only after the game begins. This finding extends the classic result by Kamenica and Gai塔rre (2011), in which the optimal mechanism was shown to be a convex combination of a "full revelation" (interim) scheme and a "no signal" (pooling) scheme. Our work generalizes this by providing an exact characterization of the entire convex polytope of optimal mechanisms, not merely as a combination of two specific extreme points.

Our methodology relies on a novel geometric approach that leverages the convexity of the set of Bayes-plausible mechanisms. We introduce a new concept of "canonical" mechanisms, where the mechanism designer commits to a specific signaling scheme for every possible signal received by agents. We prove that the polytope of optimal mechanisms consists entirely of convex combinations of these canonical mechanisms. This allows the mechanism designer to commit to a linear combination of various Bayes-plausible signaling schemes, even when the agents act sequentially.

Furthermore, we establish a "No Free Lunch" theorem for mechanism design, showing that if the mechanism designer cannot commit to a signaling scheme, they can only achieve a "No Signal" mechanism. This result highlights the critical importance of the designer's ability to commit in information design.

Finally, we apply our geometric insights to a classic example: the "Bayesian persuasion" model where a receiver chooses an action based on a state of the world, and a sender can send a signal. We show that the mechanism design space for the "Bayesian persuasion" problem is equivalent to the polytope of "Bayesian Correlated Distributions" defined by Kamenica and Gai塔rre (2011). This equivalence allows us to characterize the entire polytope of optimal mechanisms for the sender using the mechanism design framework.

This study introduces a novel approach to estimating gradients within a widely used particle weight function, the spline96 kernel, which is defined by a discontinuity at its origin. The new technique employs a "virtual smoothing" strategy, applying a temporary smoothing function to the weight function to facilitate gradient estimation. This method effectively circumvents the discontinuity, thereby eliminating the need for ad hoc rules that previously caused significant inaccuracies. The proposed approach is straightforward, computationally efficient, and robust. Numerical tests confirm its accuracy and demonstrate its superiority over existing methods. Furthermore, the method's effectiveness is illustrated through a comprehensive SPH simulation of a dam break scenario. These findings suggest that the virtual smoothing technique can be readily adapted to other discontinuous weight functions. Additionally, the method can be integrated into other SPH frameworks, such as those utilizing artificial smoothing or hybrid approaches. Finally, the implementation details are provided in an open-source Python library. This work represents a significant contribution to the field of smoothed particle hydrodynamics. This system comprises a two-dimensional honeycomb lattice of spin-1/2 fermions interacting with a two-dimensional honeycomb lattice of itinerant spins, where the latter are coupled to the former via the RKKY interaction. Our findings indicate that the system's phase diagram is governed by a unique quantum critical point (QCP) that separates a ferromagnetic insulator (FMI) from a spin liquid (SL). In the FMI phase, the itinerant spins form a ferromagnetic state, while the valence spins exhibit a Mott insulator phase characterized by a triangular lattice of spin-1/2 fermions. Conversely, in the SL phase, the itinerant spins display a spiral spin liquid state, and the valence spins form a triangular lattice Fermi liquid with a Fermi surface composed of two disconnected pockets. Notably, the Mott insulator and the spiral spin liquid coexist at the QCP, where the valence fermions develop a small Fermi surface consisting of two disconnected pockets. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the QCP is a quantum critical point of the 3D Ising universality class, despite the absence of any obvious Ising-like symmetry in the system. This research offers a new pathway for investigating quantum criticality in strongly correlated systems. Additionally, the proposed model provides a framework for understanding the phase diagram of the itinerant ferromagnet Fe$_{1-x}$Co$_x$Sn. This paper introduces a novel framework for analyzing the public health compliance game, which involves interactions between individuals and the government. This study examines QPPs within the hard X-ray (HXR) emission of a flare linked to a coronal mass ejection (CME) by applying a 1-second cadence to RHESSI and SDO/AIA data. We employed a Bayesian block algorithm to identify QPPs in the HXR light curve, revealing a pattern of 1-second brightening and dimming events. By analyzing the temporal and spatial characteristics of QPPs in HXR, EUV, and radio emissions alongside CME kinematics, we propose that the QPPs result from the interaction between the CME flux rope and magnetic reconnection sites. Specifically, the CME flux rope's expansion and the associated Alfvén wave excitation generate a series of reconnection sites, creating a quasi-periodic structure. Furthermore, the presence of QPPs in EUV and radio emissions, alongside the CME's kinematics, supports the hypothesis that these phenomena are driven by CME flux rope dynamics. Consequently, we conclude that the QPPs in this flare are caused by the coupling between the CME flux rope and the reconnection process. This work offers a novel perspective on the origins of solar flare QPPs and highlights the potential of using radio observations to investigate the dynamics of CME flux ropes. Additionally, we suggest that the QPPs observed in this study may serve as a precursor to the CME. Finally, we recommend that future investigations into the QPPs of CMEs utilize radio observations to better understand the dynamics of CME flux ropes. This research is significant for advancing our understanding of solar flares and CMEs, as well as for improving space weather forecasting. **Introduction**

Anomaly detection, also known as outlier detection, involves identifying data points that deviate significantly from the majority of the dataset. These points are often referred to as anomalies, outliers, or novelties. The field of outlier detection is vast, with applications in diverse domains such as fraud detection, fault diagnosis, and more.

The primary objective of this paper is to present a new outlier detection method based on training a neural network to reconstruct input data. The underlying principle is to train a neural network to reconstruct inputs with a controlled low error. Outliers are then detected by identifying data points where the reconstruction error surpasses a defined threshold. This approach is intuitive and straightforward, and the paper provides a detailed analysis of its mathematical underpinnings.

The proposed method is evaluated using both synthetic and real-world datasets. Results show that the method performs competitively compared to state-of-the-art outlier detection techniques. Additionally, the approach is demonstrated to be effective for feature extraction in the context of subspace-based outlier detection.

The paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews related work. Section 3 introduces the proposed outlier detection method. Section 4 presents experimental results. Finally, Section 5 offers concluding remarks.

Outlier detection is a well-established field with numerous existing methods. This section briefly outlines the most common approaches.

We demonstrate that this transition is driven by the interplay between topological defects and domain walls. This research offers new insights into the dynamics of the single-to-multiphase transition in two-dimensional systems. Ultimately, our findings may contribute to a deeper understanding of the dynamics of topological defects in other physical systems. This paper introduces a novel threat known as "backdoor poisoning," where a malicious participant in a federated learning environment inserts a backdoor into the globally aggregated model. This study presents a high-precision measurement of the lepton charge asymmetry ($A_{\rm ch}$) in the dimuon decay channel of Z bosons decaying to muon pairs, utilizing data from the ATLAS detector at the LHC with an integrated luminosity of 139 fb$^{-1}$ recorded at $\sqrt{s}$ = 13 TeV. This study examines the dynamics of a single electron confined to a two-dimensional lattice. We demonstrate that the system's behavior is dictated by the ratio of the electron-lattice coupling strength to the interaction energy. Regulation (GDPR), have introduced a right to be forgotten, enabling individuals to demand the deletion of their personal data. However, implementing this right presents significant challenges for organizations, particularly when data has been aggregated into machine learning models. This paper introduces a novel, efficient, and privacy-preserving method for removing sensitive data from pre-trained deep neural networks. Our approach utilizes a differentially private model inversion technique that is compatible with any existing architecture. We validate the method's effectiveness through extensive experiments across various deep learning models, including convolutional neural networks and long short-term memory networks, as well as different data modalities such as images, text, and time series. The results demonstrate that our technique successfully eliminates the influence of individual data points on model performance while maintaining minimal impact on overall predictive accuracy. Furthermore, the method is highly efficient, requiring only a few minutes of computation time. To the best of our knowledge, this represents the first differentially private solution capable of removing specific data points from pre-trained models. This study investigates the formation of Earth-like atmospheres on rocky exoplanets orbiting M-dwarf stars, specifically examining the impact of stellar activity. We conducted 3D hydrodynamic simulations of exoplanet atmospheres, varying the host star's activity level, the planet's mass, and its orbital distance. Our results indicate that for rocky planets within the habitable zone of active M-dwarfs, atmospheric mass loss is substantial, leading to the complete stripping of atmospheres for planets with initial masses below 0.8 Earth masses. Conversely, planets with initial masses exceeding 0.8 Earth masses can retain atmospheres, provided they are not exposed to extreme stellar activity. Furthermore, we found that atmospheric mass loss is highly sensitive to the planet's orbital distance, with the most significant effects occurring within 0.1 AU of the host star. These findings suggest that stellar activity plays a critical role in the formation of Earth-like atmospheres around rocky planets. Consequently, the presence of an atmosphere on a rocky planet within the habitable zone of an active M-dwarf may indicate that the planet is more massive than Earth. Additionally, our results imply that rocky planets in the habitable zone of active M-dwarfs are more likely to possess Earth-like atmospheres than those orbiting inactive stars. Ultimately, these findings have significant implications for the search for habitable exoplanets around M-dwarfs. Future research should prioritize the study of exoplanet atmospheres around active M-dwarfs to better understand the role of stellar activity in planetary habitability. By considering the influence of stellar activity, we can refine our models of planetary atmospheres and enhance our search for habitable worlds. a seller offers a fixed set of products to a customer, each priced by the seller or randomized by a third party. The seller's objective is to maximize the expected revenue by strategically disclosing information about the assortment to influence the customer's valuation. We examine three specific scenarios: (1) the seller knows the customer's valuation distribution and can either commit to prices beforehand or set them dynamically; (2) the seller lacks knowledge of the valuation distribution but can commit to a price distribution for each item; and (3) the seller does not know the valuation distribution and cannot commit to price distributions, instead choosing prices on the spot. Our findings indicate that in all three settings, the seller can achieve the optimal revenue by employing a "price-then-reveal" strategy, where prices are determined before the customer's valuation is known. Furthermore, we demonstrate that for the first scenario, the optimal revenue can be computed in polynomial time. Finally, we explore the implications of these results for practical applications such as dynamic pricing and online advertising. In all cases, the seller's optimal approach involves setting prices that maximize expected margins and selecting assortments to maximize expected utility. Notably, the seller's marginal cost and the seller's marginal valuation for each item are irrelevant to this optimization. Consequently, the refined assortment optimization problem offers a more realistic framework for understanding seller behavior in dynamic pricing and online advertising contexts. Additionally, our results suggest that the refined assortment optimization problem may be more tractable than the original assortment optimization problem, where the seller must commit to prices for all items in the assortment. This tractability stems from the fact that the refined problem does not require the seller to account for the customer's valuation of every item in the assortment. Instead, the customer only needs to determine the value of their most preferred item within the assortment. This simplification allows the seller to focus on maximizing the expected utility of the customer's valuation for the most attractive item in the assortment, rather than the utility of the valuation for every item. This simplification enables the seller to identify the optimal assortment and prices more efficiently. In summary, our findings indicate that the refined assortment optimization problem is both more realistic and more tractable than the original problem, making it a valuable tool for optimizing dynamic pricing and online advertising strategies. By leveraging the "price-then-reveal" strategy, sellers can achieve optimal revenue with greater efficiency and accuracy. This research advances our understanding of the complexities involved in dynamic pricing and online advertising and provides a new framework for optimizing revenue in these fields. This work extends a previous abstract investigation into the relationship between higher-order probabilistic automata and higher-order type theory, showing how the formalisms of $\mu$-CCP and $\lambda$-VTP relate to each other. Furthermore, we establish a denotational semantics for $\mu$-CCP utilizing a novel full abstract model based on continuous multisets, which we prove to be semantically equivalent to the continuous domains constructed by Plotkin. This equivalence is significant because it allows the transition from a probabilistic calculus to a type-theoretic framework, thereby enabling the application of the extensive body of type-theoretic literature to the study of probabilistic systems. We also show that the approach of modeling $\mu$-CCP as a category of continuous multisets aligns with the work of Hofmann and Plotkin on probabilistic effects. Finally, we outline a connection between $\mu$-CCP and the probabilistic variant of the $\pi$-calculus proposed by Fiore, Panangaden, and Tang. This variant, which permits probabilistic internal nondeterminism, is closely related to $\mu$-CCP, though the two are not identical. The primary distinction lies in the fact that $\mu$-CCP does not incorporate the parallel operator, which is essential for modeling the probabilistic synchronization inherent in the probabilistic $\pi$-calculus. Consequently, we also address the challenge of integrating $\mu$-CCP with the $\pi$-calculus. We propose a straightforward solution by introducing a parallel operator to $\mu$-CCP, thereby extending the calculus to encompass probabilistic synchronization. We show that this extension is both natural and consistent with established methods for modeling the $\pi$-calculus within $\mu$-CCP. Furthermore, we prove that the resulting calculus is both sound and complete with respect to a suitable category of continuous multisets. This result is achieved by defining a novel functorial approach to constructing continuous multisets, which facilitates the construction of a full abstract model for the extended calculus. This approach is inspired by the work of Hofmann and Plotkin on probabilistic effects. We also discuss the relationship between $\mu$-CCP and the probabilistic $\pi$-calculus, highlighting the necessity of the proposed extension. The paper concludes with a discussion of the implications of these results for the broader field of probabilistic process calculi.

This study employs a rigorous statistical framework to evaluate the reliability of FC in both healthy controls and individuals with schizophrenia. We introduce a novel method for assessing inter-rater reliability in FC data, which is then applied to a cohort of 102 participants comprising 56 healthy controls and 46 patients diagnosed with schizophrenia. Our findings indicate that the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) for the whole-brain FC matrix is approximately 0.01 for healthy controls and 0.02 for schizophrenia patients. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the ICC values for the top 10% of most reliable connections are roughly 0.01 and 0.03, respectively, for the two groups. These results suggest that the most reliable FC connections in both healthy controls and schizophrenia patients are predominantly located in the cerebellum. Consequently, our findings imply that the reliability of FC in identifying intrinsic brain organization is low, regardless of whether the subject is healthy or has schizophrenia. This study offers new insights into the reliability of FC and its impact on intrinsic brain organization, ultimately underscoring the need for further research into the reliability of FC. Additionally, the proposed methodological approach for estimating inter-rater reliability in FC data can be readily adapted for use in other fields. We anticipate that this research will advance the understanding of the reliability of FC in identifying intrinsic brain organization.
